text.p: Cameroon's government has postponed parliamentary elections planned for early March following opposition party complaints that their militants had not had enough time to register.

A government order, issued on Friday, said the aim was to prevent tension and street clashes that had characterised previous elections. It followed a stormy meeting between opposition leaders and government officials.

"The government, having carefully studied the slow pace witnessed in the registration exercise, has decided to postpone the elections for several weeks to allow the electorate to register," Andre Tsoungui, deputy-premier in charge of territorial administration, said in the order.
He said that another reason for the postponement was to allow time to set up a constitutional council to proclaim results and vet any complaints from candidates.

The opposition has demanded an independent national electoral commission but a spokesman for the Social Democratic Front of John Fru Ndi, one of the main opposition parties, said they would not take their campaign to the streets.
"We are not going to confront the authorities by going on the streets for any violent demonstration. We have developed some new strategies," the spokesman said.

The election will be the second parliamentary poll since Cameroon's sometimes turbulent transition to multi-party democracy began in 1990. Part of the opposition boycotted the 1992 poll. President Paul Biya's supporters secured a majority then after allying with a minor party.
Biya, who took over from independence president Ahmadou Ahidjo in 1982, faces a presidential election later this year.
